summary: Looks at case studies of Internet protocols to ask which factors contribute to or hinder a protocol's success. The aim is to offer guidance for future protocol design work. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Some inventions catch on and others do not. This paper studies old ones to guess why, so new inventors can learn from them.

questions: how should i design a protocol to succeed
what matters more technical quality or easy deployment
subtitle: Identifying why some Internet protocols succeed and others fail

tldr.problem: Many Internet protocols have been designed, but some succeed widely while others fail. Understanding the factors behind success can improve future protocol design.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC analyzes case studies of successful and failed protocols (TCP, IPv4, SSH, multicast, etc.) to identify the critical factors affecting adoption and deployment.
tldr.outcome: Initial success primarily depends on meeting a real need and incremental deployability. Wild success requires extensibility, no scalability bounds, and security. Good technical design matters less initially than often assumed.

today: RFC 5218 is Informational and has not been obsoleted. It remains a valuable reference for protocol designers, helping answer fundamental questions about what makes protocols succeed in practice rather than in theory.

sections.title: What Makes Protocols Successful
sections.content:
The Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) has defined hundreds of protocols over the decades, yet not all achieve widespread adoption. This RFC examines what distinguishes successful protocols from failed ones using historical case studies.

A successful protocol meets its original goals and sees wide deployment. A wildly successful one exceeds its design goals, either by being used in scenarios far beyond its original purpose or at scales much greater than intended. For example, HTTP was designed for document delivery, but has become the backbone for web services and content delivery at global scale.
sections.eli5: Some protocols like TCP work everywhere. Others only work in specific places. The successful ones are the ones that many programs use.

sections.title: Two Kinds of Success Factors
sections.content:
The RFC identifies initial success factors that enable a protocol to gain adoption, and wild success factors that allow it to exceed its original design.

Initial success depends on seven factors: meeting a real need with positive net value, being incrementally deployable without requiring universal coordination, having freely available open code, freedom from usage restrictions and patents, openly available specifications, open maintenance processes, and good technical design. Of these, evidence from case studies shows that the first two—addressing a real problem and incremental deployability—are the most critical. Surprisingly, technical quality ranks low initially.

Wild success factors include extensibility (the ability to add new features), absence of hard scalability limits, and adequately mitigated security threats. These factors do not significantly affect initial success but determine whether a protocol can grow far beyond its original scope.
sections.eli5: To start out, a protocol needs to solve a real problem and be easy for people to add slowly without changing everything. To grow big, it needs to be flexible and not hit limits that stop it from working at large scale.

sections.title: Case Study Examples
sections.content:
The RFC presents eight case studies. HTTP/HTML succeeded over Gopher and FTP because it provided greater value (support for forms enabled commerce), incrementally deployable clients, and excellent extensibility for new media types and technologies. IPv4 won over IPX partly because BSD Unix distributions shipped with open source IPv4 code, while IPX was proprietary. SSH succeeded over alternatives like Kerberized telnet and IPsec because it aligned costs and benefits (SSH worked at the edges without requiring infrastructure changes), deployed incrementally, and came with open code early on.

Inter-domain IP multicast, by contrast, failed because it lacked positive net value (cost-benefit alignment was poor for routers and applications), required coordination across organizations, and had poor incremental deployability. Wireless Application Protocol (WAP) failed due to restricted access, patents, poor specifications, lack of open code, and poor user experience.
sections.eli5: TCP beat competing protocols because it had free code that anyone could use. WAP failed because it charged money, was hard to get, and did not work well. Email won because it solved a real problem and anyone could set it up.

sections.title: Why Good Design Is Not Enough
sections.content:
A striking finding is that technical design quality has minimal impact on initial success. Many successful protocols—NAT, WEP, HTTP/1.0—had acknowledged technical flaws and were underspecified. NAT lacked a clear standard, leading to unpredictable behavior, yet succeeded because it provided immediate value (address sharing) that deployers could implement unilaterally.

Technically superior alternatives often lose if they lack open code, open specifications, or freedom from restrictions. IPX was arguably more elegant than IPv4 initially, yet IPv4 won. This suggests that the path to implementation and deployment matters more than design purity. Industry actors choose openness and ease of adoption over technical perfection when competing proposals offer comparable functionality.
sections.eli5: Even broken protocols can work if many people use them. A perfect protocol that costs money or is hard to get will lose to a sloppy one that is free and easy to deploy.

sections.title: Deployment Strategies and Lessons
sections.content:
The RFC concludes with guidance for protocol designers. When evaluating a new protocol, ask: Does it fill a real gap? Are there implementers ready to deploy it? Are there customers willing to adopt it? Can complexity be reduced to lower costs? Is there a killer app, or does it work within existing unmodified applications? Is it extensible enough to address future shortcomings?

For protocols that initially seem unlikely to succeed, the document recommends letting the market decide first rather than forcing standardization. Allowing multiple competing proposals and letting implementers choose can surface the most deployable option. The IETF focuses on design quality, which is important for long-term stability and wild success, but initial success depends on factors outside a standards body's direct control: open availability, low adoption barriers, and alignment of incentives with deployment.
sections.eli5: To make a new protocol win, make it easy to build, make it solve a real problem, and give away the code for free. Do not wait for perfect design—let users try different ideas and pick the one that works.

items.title: Real Need

items.title: Incremental Deployment
items.text: Early adopters get benefit even without universal support.
